title: Deploying a Site
summary: Put your site on the internet for free with GitHub Pages, Netlify or Vercel.

lessons.title: Deploying with GitHub Pages

concept.text:
Deploying means copying your site's files to a server that is always on, so that anyone can reach it at a public address. **GitHub Pages** does this free of charge for any GitHub repository: push your files and they are published.

It hosts **static** sites: HTML, CSS, JavaScript and images that are sent to the browser as they are. That covers portfolios, documentation, landing pages and the built output of React or Vue apps. It cannot run server-side code or a database.
concept.analogy: Your site on your laptop is a poster rolled up in your bedroom. Deploying is pinning it to a public notice board that never closes. GitHub Pages is a free notice board attached to the filing cabinet (repository) where you already keep your work.

visual.caption: From your computer to a public URL.

steps.title: Put the site in a repository
steps.text: The home page must be named `index.html` and sit at the top level (or in a `docs` folder).
steps.code:
git init
git add .
git commit -m "First version of my site"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/USERNAME/my-site.git
git push -u origin main

steps.title: Turn on Pages
steps.text: On GitHub open the repository, then **Settings, Pages**. Under **Build and deployment**, choose **Deploy from a branch**, select `main` and the `/ (root)` folder, and save.

steps.title: Visit your site
steps.text: After a minute it is live at `https://USERNAME.github.io/my-site/`. Every later push to `main` redeploys automatically.

steps.title: Fix the common problem
steps.text: If styles or images are missing, your paths probably start with `/`. A project site lives in a subfolder, so use relative paths such as `style.css` or `./images/photo.jpg`.

interactive.prompt: Order the steps to publish a site with GitHub Pages.
items: Create index.html and your other files
git init, git add ., git commit
Create a repository on GitHub and add it as the remote
Settings, Pages: deploy from the main branch

challenge.prompt: A site works on your computer, but on GitHub Pages at `https://sam.github.io/portfolio/` the CSS does not load. The HTML contains `<link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/style.css">`. Why does it fail, and what is the fix?
challenge.hint: Work out the full URL the browser requests for a path that starts with a slash.
challenge.solution:
A path starting with `/` is resolved from the **domain root**, so the browser requests `https://sam.github.io/css/style.css`. The file is really at `https://sam.github.io/portfolio/css/style.css`, so the request returns 404.

**Fix**: use a relative path with no leading slash: `href="css/style.css"`. The same applies to images and scripts.

takeaways: GitHub Pages hosts static sites free, straight from a repository.
Push to main and the site redeploys automatically.
Use relative paths, because project sites live in a subfolder.

lessons.title: Netlify and Vercel

concept.text:
**Netlify** and **Vercel** are hosting platforms built for modern front-end projects. You connect a Git repository once. From then on, every push triggers a build and a deployment to a global CDN, usually in under a minute. This is called **continuous deployment**.

Beyond static files, they add **preview deployments** (a unique URL for every pull request), **serverless functions** for backend code, environment variables for secrets, custom domains and automatic HTTPS, all with generous free tiers.
concept.analogy: GitHub Pages is a self-service photocopier: reliable and free, but it only copies what you give it. Netlify and Vercel are a full print shop: hand over the raw files and they assemble, print and deliver worldwide, and give you a proof to check before the final run.

steps.title: Push the project to GitHub
steps.text: Both platforms deploy from a Git repository, so start there.

steps.title: Import the repository
steps.text: Sign in to Netlify or Vercel with GitHub, choose **Add new site** or **New project**, and pick the repository. The platform detects the framework.

steps.title: Confirm the build settings
steps.text: For a Vite project these are the usual values. A plain HTML site needs no build command.
steps.code:
Build command:     npm run build
Output directory:  dist

steps.title: Add environment variables
steps.text: Put API keys in the dashboard's environment settings, never in the repository. Remember that anything shipped to the browser is public, so truly secret keys belong in a serverless function.

steps.title: Add a custom domain
steps.text: Add your domain in the dashboard and create the DNS records it shows you. HTTPS certificates are issued and renewed automatically.

challenge.prompt: You have a React site built with Vite that calls a weather API needing a secret key. Describe how you would deploy it so that the site auto-updates on push and the key stays private.
challenge.hint: Two parts: the hosting pipeline, and where the key is used.
challenge.solution:
1. Push the project to GitHub and import it into Netlify or Vercel. Build command `npm run build`, output directory `dist`. Every push to `main` now redeploys, and each pull request gets a preview URL.

2. Create a **serverless function**, for example `/api/weather`, that reads the key from an **environment variable** and calls the weather API on the server.

3. Set the variable in the platform's dashboard, not in the repository.

4. Have the React app call `/api/weather` instead of the weather service directly. The key never reaches the browser.

takeaways: Connect a repository once and every push deploys automatically.
Preview deployments let you test changes on a real URL before merging.
Keep secrets in environment variables and use them only in serverless functions.
